title: Advanced Ingress & Network Policy Patterns ⚙️
description: Canary releases, URL rewrites, and combining policies for zero‑trust.

slides.title: Canary Deployments with Ingress 🐤
slides.content:
# Gradual traffic shifting

You can release a new version to a small percentage of users using Ingress annotations (nginx‑specific):

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: app-canary
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: "10"
spec:
  rules:
  - host: app.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: app-v2
            port:
              number: 80
```

10% of traffic goes to `app-v2`, the rest to the main Ingress (without canary).

slides.title: Canary Example Setup
slides.content: You need two Ingresses sharing the same host: one main, one canary.
slides.codeSnippet:
# Main Ingress (no canary annotation)
kubectl apply -f app-main.yaml
# Canary Ingress (with annotation)
kubectl apply -f app-canary.yaml

quizData.question: Which annotation enables canary traffic splitting in NGINX Ingress?
quizData.explanation: The canary annotation is specific to the NGINX controller.

slides.title: URL Rewrites and Redirects ↩️
slides.content:
## Modify paths before hitting the backend

Using NGINX annotations:
- `rewrite-target`: rewrite the request URI before sending to backend.
- `ssl-redirect`: force HTTPS.

```yaml
annotations:
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /$2
spec:
  rules:
  - host: app.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /old-api(/|$)(.*)
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: new-api-svc
            port:
              number: 80
```

Requests to `/old-api/users` become `/users` to the backend.

slides.title: NetworkPolicy with Namespace Selectors 🏢
slides.content:
## Cross‑namespace communication control

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-monitoring
  namespace: prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          purpose: monitoring
    ports:
    - port: 9090
```

Allows pods in namespaces labeled `purpose=monitoring` to access port 9090 on backend Pods.

slides.title: Label a Namespace for NetworkPolicy
slides.codeSnippet:
kubectl label namespace monitoring purpose=monitoring
kubectl apply -f np-allow-monitoring.yaml

slides.title: Combining Ingress and NetworkPolicy 🧱
slides.content:
## Defense in depth

Use Ingress for L7 routing (host/path) and NetworkPolicy for L3/L4 restrictions. For example:
- Ingress: route `api.example.com` to `api-svc`.
- NetworkPolicy: allow traffic to `api-svc` only from the Ingress controller’s namespace.

This ensures even if an attacker compromises a Pod in another namespace, they cannot bypass the Ingress controller.

quizData.question: Why would you restrict ingress to a backend Service to only the Ingress controller’s namespace?

options.text: To force all external traffic through the Ingress controller (no direct Pod access)

quizData.explanation: It enforces that only the Ingress controller can route to the backend, preventing bypass.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use Cilium for eBPF‑based policies

Cilium provides fine‑grained L7 policies (HTTP method, API path) beyond standard NetworkPolicies. It also offers deep observability.
